name: Treaty with the Cherokee, 1791 (Treaty of Holston)
promises: Article 7: the United States solemnly guaranteed to the Cherokee nation all their lands not ceded by this treaty.
Article 8: any United States citizen who settled on Cherokee lands would forfeit the protection of the United States, and the Cherokees could punish him as they pleased.
An annual payment for the ceded land, raised to $1,500 by the additional article of February 17, 1792.
A defined boundary between the Cherokee and the United States, and United States citizens to enter Cherokee country only with a passport.

breaches.what: The Supreme Court held that Georgia's law extending its jurisdiction over Cherokee territory, under which the missionary Samuel Worcester was imprisoned, was void as repugnant to the treaties of Hopewell and Holston, and that Georgia's laws had no force in the Cherokee Nation.

source.title: Worcester v. Georgia, 31 U.S. 515 (1832)
source.publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School

breaches.quote: a distinct community occupying its own territory, with boundaries accurately described, in which the laws of Georgia can have no force

breaches.what: The National Park Service states that Georgia ignored the Worcester ruling and that the federal judicial and executive branches did nothing to enforce it, and that the Cherokee were forcibly removed within a few years of the 1835 treaty.
breaches.whoFoundIt: National Park Service, Fort Smith National Historic Site

source.title: Cherokee Relations with US Government Before Removal

breaches.quote: Georgia simply ignored the ruling and the judicial and executive branches of the federal government did nothing to enforce it.

landTaken: The lands guaranteed by Article 7 east of the Mississippi were ceded by later treaties, finally by the Treaty of New Echota (1835); see kappler-447.
compensation: No payment for the breach of the Article 7 guarantee was located.
today: Not researched beyond the removal; see the Treaty of New Echota (kappler-447).

nationVoice.summary: The Nation's history describes the removal forced on it after the 1835 treaty, when the Army rounded Cherokee people into camps in 1838.

sources.title: Treaty with the Cherokee, 1791 (Kappler, vol. 2, p. 29)

openQuestions: Worcester v. Georgia found that Georgia, a state, acted against the treaty; the federal failure to enforce rests on the National Park Service's statement, not on a ruling.
The exact decision date of Worcester v. Georgia was not taken from the opinion page (it gives January Term, 1832); it is commonly given as March 3, 1832, which was not checked.
Whether the annuities under the treaty and its additional article were paid in full was not researched; Indian Claims Commission Cherokee dockets are the lead.
